newsitem.title: USA: WHEAT--U.S. HRW crop seen off to strong start.
newsitem.headline: WHEAT--U.S. HRW crop seen off to strong start.

text.p: The 1996/97 U.S. hard red winter wheat crop has gotten off to a strong start thanks to adequate subsoil moisture levels, dry planting weather and timely rains, agronomists said Thursday.
"The crop that I've seen looks really good, especially compared to last year," said Jim Shroyer, extension agronomist at Kansas State University in Manhattan, Kansas.
Shroyer recalled how at this time a year ago, the onset of mostly dry weather prevented the crop from growing and establishing tillers.
"It's dramatically different from last year," said Mark Hodges, director of the Oklahoma Wheat Commission.

"We had excellent moisture over the summer and into the fall so we've got some deep moisture levels. We've also had fairly consistent surface moisture, which has allowed some good primary root development of the wheat that's been planted," Hodges said.

There were some minor problems, however. Shroyer relayed reports of leaf rust fungus in some wheat in southwest Kansas. But he said most of the fungus spores should be killed with the arrival of sub-zero winter temperatures.
Bill Nelson, executive director of the Texas Wheat Commission, said the wheat in his state was not off to a "perfect start" because some areas of southern Texas were still short of moisture.
Nelson cited the latest weekly Texas crop report, released Monday by the Texas Department of Agricultural Statistics, which rated the wheat at 81 percent of normal.
The report said 78 percent of all Texas wheat acreage had emerged, compared to 36 percent a year ago and 44 percent for the five-year average.

The weekly Oklahoma crop report said 57 percent of the wheat acreage had emerged, versus 36 percent a year ago and 54 percent on average. Oklahoma wheat was rated 78 percent good to excellent, 20 percent fair and two percent poor.

In Kansas, traditionally the number one winter wheat producing state, the wheat was 74 percent emerged compared to 69 percent last year and the average of 70 percent. The weekly report rated Kansas' wheat crop as 88 percent good to excellent and 12 percent fair.
